facts.claim: The Black Death reached Europe through Sicilian ports
facts.context: Ships from the Black Sea carried plague into Messina in October 1347.
facts.goDeeper: Within three years it had reached almost every corner of Europe, including Iceland and Greenland.

facts.claim: The plague reached England
facts.context: It arrived in the south-west in summer 1348 and reached London by autumn.
facts.goDeeper: Roughly half of England's population died within about two years.

facts.claim: Estimated deaths in Europe from the Black Death
facts.context: Estimates range from about 25 to 50 million in Europe, out of a population near 80 million.
facts.goDeeper: It is generally reckoned the deadliest pandemic in recorded human history.

facts.claim: Share of Europe's population killed by the Black Death
facts.context: Commonly put between 30 and 60 percent, with wide regional variation.
facts.goDeeper: Some villages vanished entirely and were never resettled; their outlines still show in English fields.

facts.claim: Venice's colony at Ragusa imposed the first recorded quarantine
facts.context: Arriving ships were isolated for thirty days, later extended to forty.
facts.goDeeper: The Italian for forty, quaranta, is where the word quarantine comes from.

facts.claim: Alexandre Yersin identified the bacterium that causes plague
facts.context: Isolated during an outbreak in Hong Kong; the organism is named Yersinia pestis after him.
facts.goDeeper: DNA recovered from medieval graves confirmed in 2011 that this was indeed the Black Death's cause.

facts.claim: The Great Plague of London killed roughly a quarter of the city
facts.context: The last major English outbreak, ending as the Great Fire swept the city in 1666.
facts.goDeeper: About 100,000 Londoners died, in a city of some 460,000.

facts.claim: The village of Eyam quarantined itself to stop the plague spreading
facts.context: Villagers agreed to cut themselves off entirely rather than let the outbreak reach neighbouring towns.
facts.goDeeper: Around a quarter to a half of Eyam died. Surrounding villages were largely spared.

facts.claim: The Plague of Justinian struck the Byzantine Empire
facts.context: An earlier pandemic of the same bacterium, beginning in 541, devastated Constantinople.
facts.goDeeper: It recurred in waves for two centuries and may have helped end Justinian's hopes of restoring the Roman Empire.

facts.claim: England passed the Statute of Labourers to hold wages at pre-plague levels
facts.context: With so many workers dead, survivors could demand higher pay. Parliament tried to freeze wages by law.
facts.goDeeper: It failed, and the resentment it caused fed into the Peasants' Revolt thirty years later.

facts.claim: The Peasants' Revolt broke out in England
facts.context: A rising against taxation and labour restrictions imposed after the plague.
facts.goDeeper: The rebels took London and met the fourteen-year-old Richard II in person before the revolt collapsed.

facts.claim: Typical days between infection with bubonic plague and first symptoms
facts.context: Usually two to six days, after which fever and swollen lymph nodes appear.
facts.goDeeper: Untreated bubonic plague kills a majority of those infected. With modern antibiotics, most survive.

facts.claim: Years it took Europe's population to return to pre-plague levels
facts.context: Most estimates put full demographic recovery at around two centuries.
facts.goDeeper: Repeated outbreaks through the 14th and 15th centuries kept knocking the recovery back.

facts.claim: The Black Death spread only through rats and their fleas
facts.context: Rat fleas were one route, but the speed of spread suggests human fleas, body lice and person-to-person pneumonic transmission also mattered.
facts.goDeeper: The plague spread through Iceland, which had no black rats at all.

facts.claim: The beaked plague-doctor mask dates from the Black Death itself
facts.context: The costume was devised in the 17th century, roughly 300 years after the Black Death.
facts.goDeeper: The beak was packed with herbs, on the theory that disease travelled in bad air.

facts.claim: The rhyme 'Ring a Ring o' Roses' is a proven reference to the plague
facts.context: Folklorists reject the connection. The rhyme is not recorded until the 19th century, and the plague reading appears only after the Second World War.
facts.goDeeper: It is one of the most widely repeated pieces of false etymology in English.

facts.claim: Plague still infects people today
facts.context: A few thousand cases are reported worldwide each year, including a handful annually in the western United States.
facts.goDeeper: Treated early with antibiotics it is now usually survivable.

facts.claim: Jewish communities were blamed and attacked during the Black Death
facts.context: False accusations of well-poisoning led to massacres across the Rhineland and beyond in 1348 and 1349.
facts.goDeeper: Pope Clement VI issued bulls condemning the attacks and pointing out that Jews were dying of the plague too.

facts.claim: People at the time called it the Black Death
facts.context: Contemporaries called it the pestilence or the great mortality. 'Black Death' became common in English only centuries later.
facts.goDeeper: The name may come from a mistranslation of the Latin atra mors, where atra means both black and terrible.

facts.claim: The plague reshaped European art toward images of death
facts.context: The danse macabre and the memento mori spread widely in the decades after the pandemic.
facts.goDeeper: Skeletons leading popes, kings and peasants alike away made a pointed argument about equality in death.
